property_summary: For any caller address X, the correct contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer set at construction), whereas the mutant returns the caller (msg.sender) for some callers, violating that invariant.

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds for non-zero newOwner and reverts (call returns false) when newOwner == address(0) in the reference; the mutant that removed the require allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the owner, calling transferOwnership with newOwner == address(0) must revert (i.e., fail) in the correct contract, while the mutant that removed the require allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed; the property asserts that attempting to transfer ownership to zero address always fails for the reference.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) reverts when newOwner == address(0) on the reference contract (it forbids transferring ownership to the zero address); the mutant removed that check and therefore allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed for some input.

For any owner caller and any newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the owner() getter must equal newOwner only if newOwner != address(0); the reference reverts when newOwner==address(0) so owner() cannot become zero, whereas the mutant allows owner() to become address(0) — so assert that owner()!=address(0) after calls from the current owner (the reference always preserves non-zero owner), which the mutant violates for some fuzzed newOwner inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner, invoking transferOwnership(newOwner) either reverts when newOwner==address(0) (reference) or — in the mutant — may succeed and set owner() to address(0); thus the reference guarantees that after any transferOwnership call by the owner, owner() is never address(0) (the mutant can violate this for some newOwner).

Invariant: Only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership(newOwner) (call returns/does not revert) for any newOwner != address(0); the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction so some non-owner caller can successfully change owner, violating this rule.
Only the contract owner can change rewardDistributor (setRewardDistributor) — i.e., after calling setRewardDistributor by msg.sender, owner() must still equal the caller that set it.
Only the current rewardDistributor or the contract owner can have their call to setRewardDistributor succeed (i.e., the call reverts iff sender is neither owner nor current rewardDistributor).
The call to setRewardDistributor(caller) must succeed iff the test's msg.sender is either the contract owner or the current rewardDistributor.
The call to setRewardDistributor(caller) must revert iff this test's msg.sender is neither the contract owner nor the current rewardDistributor.
The call to setRewardDistributor(caller) must succeed exactly when this test's msg.sender is either the contract owner or the current rewardDistributor.

Invariant: Only the contract owner can change rewardDistributor via setRewardDistributor; the mutant allows the current rewardDistributor (not owner) to change it, so for some fuzzed caller the mutant will permit a non-owner to update rewardDistributor while the reference rejects such a caller.

For any address newToken added via addReward by the contract owner, the rewardDistributor remains unchanged by that call in the reference; the mutant (which allows the current rewardDistributor to call setRewardDistributor) can lead to rewardDistributor differing after addReward when an external reward token's transfer triggers a callback that calls setRewardDistributor during notifyRewardAmount/transferFrom, so the invariant 'rewardDistributor stays the same across addReward' is violated by the mutant for some adversarial token behavior.

For any deployed C, calling addReward(token) does not change rewardDistributor in the correct contract; the mutant can have rewardDistributor changed during addReward if a malicious reward token's transferFrom calls back into C.setRewardDistributor (since mutant allows current rewardDistributor to call it), so rewardDistributor may differ after addReward.

For any address newToken passed to addReward by the contract owner, addReward never changes rewardDistributor in the reference implementation; the mutant can have rewardDistributor changed during addReward if a malicious ERC20's transferFrom triggers a call into setRewardDistributor (mutant allows current rewardDistributor to call), so rewardDistributor may differ after addReward.

For any inputs, calling addReward(...) as the contract owner never changes rewardDistributor in the correct contract; the mutant can have rewardDistributor changed during addReward if an ERC20 token's transferFrom re-enters and calls setRewardDistributor (since mutant allows rewardDistributor to call it), so rewardDistributor may differ after addReward.
Only the owner can change the rewardDistributor (so non-owner attempts do not alter rewardDistributor).
